interviewQuestions.question: Why does pure content-based filtering lead to a filter bubble?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd explain the mechanism first: content-based filtering builds a user profile from the features of items they've already liked, then recommends whatever is most similar to that profile. That similarity computation is the entire recommendation logic — there's no step anywhere that looks at what *other* users liked. So if a user's history is all thrillers, the profile vector sits in thriller-space, and everything returned is more thriller.

Concretely: on a news app, if someone reads three articles about one political topic, pure content-based filtering will keep feeding them that topic indefinitely — it has no way to know that readers with a similar profile also engaged heavily with a totally different topic, because it never looks at other readers at all. That cross-user leap requires collaborative signal.

The fix in practice is hybridization: blend in collaborative filtering or explicitly inject a diversity/exploration term into the ranking so the system occasionally surfaces something outside the profile's neighborhood.

**Testing:** whether you understand that content-based filtering's blind spot isn't a modeling weakness to tune away — it's structural, since the method by definition never consults other users' behavior.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The filter bubble

interviewQuestions.question: Why does content-based filtering solve new-item cold start but not new-user cold start, when both seem like the same 'no data' problem on the surface?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The two cold-start cases are asymmetric because content-based filtering's core inputs are item features plus a user's own history, and a brand-new item is missing only one of those, while a brand-new user is missing the other entirely — with nothing to substitute. A new item, the moment it's added to the catalog, already has its feature vector available: genre, price, brand, or a text/image embedding of its description — none of that depends on any user having interacted with it yet. So the item can immediately be compared for similarity against existing items and slotted into recommendations right away, purely from its own attributes; this is exactly why content-based filtering is often specifically reached for to handle newly-added items in a catalog.

A new user has no equivalent substitute available. The entire recommendation mechanism depends on building a user profile vector from the features of items that user has already liked — and a user with zero history has nothing to build that profile from. There's no "item's own features" analog for a user; the method has no fallback source of signal the way new items do. This is a structural gap, not something more item features could patch, because the missing ingredient is specifically the user's own interaction history, and no amount of item metadata substitutes for that.

In practice this asymmetry is exactly why real systems don't rely on content-based filtering alone for new users — they fall back to onboarding signals (explicitly asked preferences), popularity-based defaults, or content-based similarity to whatever minimal signal exists (a single "like" during onboarding), while genuinely solving new-user cold start usually still needs something beyond pure content-based filtering.

**Testing:** whether you can explain *why* the asymmetry exists structurally, not just recite that one cold-start case is solved and the other isn't.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why the two cold-start cases aren't symmetric

interviewQuestions.question: You're building a recommender for a new product where you genuinely can't collect cross-user collaborative signal yet (privacy constraints, or too few users). How far can content-based filtering alone get you, and what would you tell the product team about its limits?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd be upfront that content-based filtering alone can get a genuinely usable first version shipped — it needs no other users' data at all, works from item features and a single user's own history, and it's the standard choice exactly when collaborative signal isn't available yet, whether from cold start or, as here, a structural constraint. For users with even a small amount of interaction history, it can produce reasonable, locally-relevant recommendations by matching item features to what that user has already engaged with.

But I'd be equally clear about what it cannot do, because these are structural limitations, not something more engineering effort fixes later. First, the filter bubble: because it only ever recommends things similar to what a user already liked, it has no mechanism for surfacing anything the user hasn't shown affinity for yet — recommendations get locally accurate but globally narrow over time, with zero serendipity, since there's no cross-user signal to say "people with similar taste unexpectedly loved this different thing." Second, it does nothing for a brand-new user with no history at all — that cold-start case needs a different mechanism (onboarding preferences, popularity defaults), since content-based filtering has no substitute for missing user history the way it does for missing item history.

Given the stated privacy/scale constraint ruling out collaborative filtering, I'd propose two mitigations that don't require cross-user data: explicit exploration built into the ranking (deliberately surface some items outside the user's current profile neighborhood on a controlled basis) and richer onboarding (ask new users directly for a few preferences rather than relying purely on inferred history) — both work within the constraint while directly addressing the two specific gaps content-based filtering leaves open.

**Testing:** whether you can honestly scope what content-based filtering can and can't do under a real constraint, rather than either overselling it or dismissing it as insufficient.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Scoping content-based filtering under a real constraint
